messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 50
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Plumber
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 73

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep
  Memory: Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
  Negative Appraisals: No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it, Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

John is a 50-year-old African man who works as a plumber. He lives in a modest home with his wife and has been married for over two decades. His life took a drastic turn six months ago when he was brutally assaulted by an unknown assailant outside his workplace. The attack left him severely shaken, both physically and mentally. John vividly remembers the night of the assault. It was just another day at work; he had completed several plumbing repairs in various apartments in the building where he worked. As he walked back to his car late that evening, a shadowy figure emerged from behind a dumpster. The assailant lunged at him with a knife and delivered several brutal slashes across his arms and chest before fleeing into the darkness. Since then, John has felt profoundly unsafe outside of his home. He only feels truly safe within the confines of his small apartment, where he can lock all doors and windows. Any unexpected movement nearby now causes an intense startle response, often leaving him hypervigilant and on edge. Even simple sounds or sudden movements make him react as if he is still in imminent danger. John's sleep has been severely disrupted since the attack. He finds it extremely difficult to fall asleep and frequently wakes up in the middle of the night with vivid images of the assault replaying in his mind. The constant visual memories are overwhelming, and he struggles to put them into words or make sense of what happened. This inability to verbalize his experience only adds to his distress. Whenever John remembers the event, a deep sense of guilt washes over him. He wonders if there was something he could have done differently to prevent the assault, further fueling his feelings of inadequacy and self-doubt. The memory haunts him in various ways—sometimes through flashbacks while working or driving, other times when he sees similar circumstances that remind him of the attack. John’s occupation as a plumber has become increasingly difficult since the incident. He avoids jobs that require him to work alone or late into the evening. This avoidance behavior has led to conflicts with his employer and colleagues who are confused by his reluctance to take on certain tasks. Over time, John's workload has diminished, and he feels less capable of performing the duties that once defined him as a skilled plumber. His wife notices the changes in John’s behavior but struggles to understand why he is so hesitant to return to work or even venture out alone. He avoids discussing the assault with her and others, finding it nearly impossible to articulate what happened. This has created a rift between them, as she feels increasingly isolated and unable to support him. John's sense of injustice compounds his distress. He believes that what happened was deeply unfair and that nothing has been done about it. The lack of resolution adds to his feelings of vulnerability and mistrust in the world around him. He is certain that he will not be able to do the right thing when faced with danger again, further exacerbating his anxiety. The cumulative impact of these symptoms finally compelled John to seek help. His wife insisted they visit a therapist after noticing significant changes in his mood and behavior over several months. John is most afraid of losing control or being unable to protect himself from another attack. He hopes that therapy will provide him with the tools he needs to regain some sense of security and trust in his abilities, ultimately allowing him to return to work and rebuild a more fulfilling life. In our initial sessions, it becomes clear that John’s trauma has profoundly altered how he perceives both himself and the world around him. His specific triggers—unexpected movement and limited safe zones—are direct reflections of his traumatic experience. The guilt, visual memories, and inability to verbalize his fears are all interconnected aspects of his struggle with PTSD. As we work together, John begins to recognize that these symptoms do not define him but rather represent a part of his life's narrative he hopes to overcome.
